sentences.text: The genus Nanuqsaurus contains only one species, Nanuqsaurus hoglundi, which is known from a partial skull and various postcranial and tooth fragments.
This animal was estimated to be about 6 meters long and weighed between 500 and 900 kilograms.
The reconstructed skull length, based on proportions of its close relatives, is 60 to 70 centimeters.
Nanuqsaurus has a distinctive edge on its head indicating it was closely related to Tyrannosaurus rex.

As a tyrannosaurine, it is diagnosed by a thin, bifurcated midline rostral process of fused parietals overlapping the frontals, elongated rostral frontals separating prefrontal and lacrimal facets, and the first two dentary teeth being much smaller than the following ones.
Evidence suggests Nanuqsaurus remained in the paleo-Arctic year-round, enduring approximately 120 days of constant winter darkness without migrating.
Given its size and cold environment, it is probable that Nanuqsaurus hoglundi was covered in a layer of hair-like feathers, as known in other tyrannosauroids.
Fossil remains of Nanuqsaurus were discovered in 2006 at the Kikak-Tegoseak Quarry in the North Slope Borough of Alaska.
The genus Nanuqsaurus was formally described and named by Anthony R. Fiorillo and Ronald S. Tykoski in 2014.
The name is derived from the Iñupiaq word nanuq, meaning "polar bear".
As the largest carnivore in its area, Nanuqsaurus was likely an apex predator.
The shape of its skull suggests it had an enlarged brain area dedicated to smell, indicating it relied heavily on scent to hunt prey, similar to Tyrannosaurus rex.
Recent studies of additional fossils suggest Nanuqsaurus was likely similar in size to large North American tyrannosaurids like Albertosaurus, rather than being a small animal as initially thought.
Some postcranial elements of Nanuqsaurus scale to approximately 7 meters in length, comparable to a juvenile Tarbosaurus.
Based on recently collected fossils, adult Nanuqsaurus specimens are estimated to have weighed over 1.9 metric tons.

Paleontologists suggest that about 70 million years ago, northern Alaska was separated from the continent of Laramidia and experienced a cold climate with long periods of darkness and light, making food hard to find.
Nanuqsaurus likely decreased in size due to a year-round decrease in food supply caused by colder temperatures.
It is proposed that Nanuqsaurus laid eggs around April to take advantage of the constant daylight and relative warmth for incubation.
Phylogenetic analysis places Nanuqsaurus as a close relative of Daspletosaurus and Tyrannosaurus within the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.
Nanuqsaurus is a member of the highly derived tyrannosaurine subfamily.
It is considered the sister taxon to a clade containing Tyrannosaurus, Tarbosaurus, and probably Zhuchengtyrannus.
Its parent group is Tyrannosaurinae.
It belongs to the family Tyrannosauridae.
Nanuqsaurus lived during the latest Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous.
Nanuqsaurus lived between 70 and 68 million years ago at the beginning of the Maastrichtian stage in what is now North America.
The Kikak-Tegoseak Quarry region of the Prince Creek Formation dates to the late early Maastrichtian, 71 to 68 million years ago.
An average age of 69.1 ± 0.3 million years found in the formation rocks suggests Nanuqsaurus lived at that time.
Its time range is the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
A 2023 thesis argued that Nanuqsaurus is a nomen dubium due to poorly resolved taxonomic validity and phylogenetic position.
Further studies have indicated that the anatomical traits used to diagnose Nanuqsaurus may not be unique to the genus.
It is debated whether the rostral parietal spur is actually present in Nanuqsaurus, as this trait is variably present across Tyrannosauridae.
